Essential hypertension for 12 years, well controlled
Right lobar intracerebral haemorrhage 4 years ago, small, managed conservatively with good recovery

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, year correct, date incorrect. MoCA 20/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span backwards, serial sevens and delayed recall (2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued). Mild anomia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent.

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent spreading sensory episodes and two years of cognitive decline, on aspirin for presumed transient ischaemic attacks
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ludovico Sarti is a 76-year-old retired headmaster referred with recurrent stereotyped episodes and cognitive decline. The episodes have occurred about ten times in the past year, are identical each time, and consist of tingling that begins in the right thumb and spreads over two to three minutes up the arm and onto the face before resolving completely. There is no jerking, no loss of awareness and no headache. They were diagnosed as transient ischaemic attacks and he was started on aspirin; they have continued unchanged, and if anything have become more frequent since. Separately, his wife reports two years of cognitive decline: he is slower, forgets conversations unless reminded of the context, has stopped managing the household accounts, and has lost the thread of the reading group he chaired. Four years ago he had a small right lobar intracerebral haemorrhage which was managed conservatively and from which he recovered well; it was attributed to hypertension, although his blood pressure has been well controlled throughout. His mother died of an intracerebral haemorrhage at 82. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.

signal_characteristics.T2: Multiple centrum semiovale perivascular spaces — the distribution associated with amyloid angiopathy rather than the basal ganglia pattern of hypertensive arteriopathy

findings.location: Mild global with posterior weighting; medial temporal lobes preserved

additional_observations: Eleven microbleeds, every one lobar, with focal cortical superficial siderosis in two sulci and a prior lobar haemorrhage: the Boston criteria version 2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy are met
There is no deep or infratentorial microbleed, which is what excludes hypertensive arteriopathy as the explanation
Centrum semiovale rather than basal ganglia perivascular space enlargement, and posteriorly weighted white matter change, are both supportive markers of amyloid angiopathy
The recurrent stereotyped spreading sensory episodes correspond to the cortical superficial siderosis and are transient focal neurological episodes, not transient ischaemic attacks
mri.impression: Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy by the Boston criteria version 2.0: multiple strictly lobar microbleeds, focal cortical superficial siderosis and a prior lobar haemorrhage, with supportive centrum semiovale perivascular spaces and posteriorly weighted white matter change. The cognitive syndrome is a vascular cognitive disorder on this substrate, and the stereotyped sensory episodes are transient focal neurological episodes arising from the siderosis.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment of dementia severity due to probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Boston criteria v2.0), with transient focal neurological episodes from cortical superficial siderosis

differential.key_features: This was the working diagnosis and the reason for the aspirin, but the episodes are stereotyped, spread over two to three minutes and are purely positive sensory phenomena — the signature of transient focal neurological episodes from cortical superficial siderosis, and the aspirin raises the risk of lobar haemorrhage

The prior haemorrhage was attributed to hypertension, but his blood pressure has been well controlled, every one of eleven microbleeds is lobar, and there is no deep or infratentorial microbleed — the distribution excludes it

The episodes spread over minutes rather than seconds, which is the migrainous-spreading rather than the epileptic pattern; siderosis can cause either, and if they persist or evolve an EEG and an antiseizure trial become reasonable

Amyloid PET is positive but cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid, medial temporal lobes are preserved and recall is cue-responsive — so coexisting Alzheimer's disease is possible but unproven and does not change management here
New stereotyped spreading sensory episodes beginning in the eighth decade in a patient with no migraine history, in the presence of cortical superficial siderosis

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Recurrent stereotyped spreading sensory episodes lasting minutes — the pattern of transient focal neurological episodes, not of transient ischaemic attacks — together with two years of cognitive decline and a prior lobar haemorrhage in a well-controlled hypertensive

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded and coagulation normal, so the bleeding tendency is vascular rather than haematological

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Eleven strictly lobar microbleeds with focal cortical superficial siderosis and a prior lobar haemorrhage — probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy by Boston criteria v2.0, with no deep microbleed

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Executive and retrieval profile with preserved recognition, consistent with a vascular cognitive disorder in a high-baseline patient

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines

optimal_actions.expected_finding: The antithrombotic decision reversed — aspirin stopped and future anticoagulation flagged as contraindicated — the episodes correctly named, and haemorrhage risk explained to the family

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture adds risk without changing management in a patient with probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy: the diagnosis is already established on imaging criteria, the antithrombotic decision follows from it, and CSF amyloid cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Recognise stereotyped, spreading, positive sensory episodes as transient focal neurological episodes rather than transient ischaemic attacks
Obtain MRI with SWI: the microbleed distribution and cortical superficial siderosis are the diagnosis
Apply the Boston criteria version 2.0 explicitly rather than describing microbleeds without classifying them
Stop antiplatelet therapy started for the misdiagnosis, because it raises the risk of lobar haemorrhage
Record prominently that anticoagulation is contraindicated in this patient
Exclude reversible causes of the cognitive decline and confirm normal coagulation
Counsel the patient and family on recurrent haemorrhage risk and on the nature of the episodes
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue or start antiplatelet therapy for these episodes — they are not ischaemic and the drug raises the haemorrhage risk
Do not anticoagulate this patient, now or in the future, without a compelling and reconsidered indication
Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the diagnosis is established on imaging and CSF cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid
Do not attribute a lobar haemorrhage to hypertension in a well-controlled patient with eleven strictly lobar microbleeds
Do not give thrombolysis in any future event without reconsidering this diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: Transient focal neurological episodes are the presenting feature of cortical superficial siderosis and are distinguished from transient ischaemic attacks by being stereotyped, recurrent, positive rather than negative in phenomenology, and spreading over minutes
The distribution rule is the whole diagnosis: strictly lobar microbleeds with siderosis is amyloid angiopathy, and a single deep microbleed would have argued for hypertensive arteriopathy instead

Misdiagnosing these episodes as transient ischaemic attacks leads directly to an antithrombotic that increases the risk of the haemorrhage the patient is already prone to — the treatment was harmful, not merely useless
Supportive markers matter: centrum semiovale rather than basal ganglia perivascular spaces, and posteriorly weighted white matter change, both point to amyloid angiopathy
Amyloid PET cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid, so a positive scan does not establish coexisting Alzheimer's disease and does not change management here

red_herrings.data_point: An existing diagnosis of recurrent transient ischaemic attacks with aspirin already prescribed
red_herrings.intended_effect: Confirms an ischaemic mechanism and keeps the patient on a drug that increases his haemorrhage risk
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The episodes are stereotyped positive sensory phenomena spreading over minutes — transient focal neurological episodes from cortical superficial siderosis — and the aspirin should be stopped

red_herrings.data_point: A previous lobar haemorrhage attributed to hypertension
red_herrings.intended_effect: Supports hypertensive arteriopathy and makes the microbleeds seem consistent with it
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: His blood pressure has been well controlled and every one of eleven microbleeds is lobar with no deep or infratentorial lesion, which is the distribution of amyloid angiopathy and not of hypertensive arteriopathy

key_educational_points: Stereotyped spreading positive sensory episodes are transient focal neurological episodes of amyloid angiopathy, not transient ischaemic attacks
Microbleed distribution — strictly lobar versus deep — decides between amyloid and hypertensive arteriopathy and thereby the antithrombotic plan
The Boston criteria version 2.0 add cortical superficial siderosis, centrum semiovale perivascular spaces and posterior white matter change as supportive markers
Amyloid PET cannot distinguish vascular from parenchymal amyloid
